metadata.title: Shannon Shakes Hands with Chernoff: Big Data Viewpoint On Channel Information Measures

extraction_notes.note: The ACE pseudocode is malformed: lines 2 and 3 both read 'Iterate until ... fails to decrease' (outer and inner loops) and the loop ends are printed as separate \STATE lines, so no nesting is syntactic. Kept lines as flat steps with loop subclass, dropped the two 'End ... Loop' lines.
The paper's findings are read off ACE transformation plots (figures not available as content); each stated observation was emitted as a numerical-rigor claim.
Corollary vs claim: the paper itself calls 'Shannon's theta^{-1} is bigger than Chernoff's' 'this corollary', so it is typed corollary although it is an inference from simulated plots.
The headline 'Shannon shakes hands with Chernoff' paragraph could be one remark; split into the claim sentence and the following physical/analogy argument as a heuristic proof.
MSC definition sentences introduce M, lambda_i and the per-symbol error together (one sentence lacks a space after its period); kept as one definition node.
Introduction restatements (mutual information, Chernoff information, the conjecture in the abstract/conclusion) and the PAC/SVM aside in Sec. 4.1 were not given separate nodes.

nodes.statement: Over the last decades, Shannon information and Chernoff information are always considered to be two kinds of channel information measures and the relation between them is that Kullback-Leibler divergence is the special case of R\'enyi divergence when alpha=1. The channel information measures deduced from them look very different even for the channel as simple as BSC. However, with the aid of the ACE algorithm, we find the inner relations between them. In fact, they are different metrics of the same physical quantity. For a channel, in a certain time, if all of its parameters are given, all of its state and properties will be determined. Thus the information about the same channel is always consistent. For example, the kilometer and centimeter are both measures of length, but they are used in different situations for convenience. Generally speaking, we do not adopt the centimeter to measure the distance between two cities.
